However,thereisamyriadoftechnicalelements that are being or could be associated with the SDF technique that are far lower in technological readiness. These elements generally fit in one or more of the following categories: • radiation sensor customization for specific applications; • software customization to achieve tailored analysis products; • incorporation of spectroscopic information into analyses; • incorporating prior and/or physics information into analyses; • contextual sensing hardware improvements; • contextual sensing data analysis advances; • enabling autonomous systems that leverage SDF; and • improving user interfaces to support and elucidate these improvements. These categories also indicate high-level avenues for development, but cannot be categorized with a TRL without discussing each specific application for which they may be developed. They may also overlap; for instance mapping of radioactive contamination prior to re-habitation of an area may require high-sensitivity radiation detectors, algorithms that are able to leverage prior information in assessment of spectroscopic information, and be operated in a many kilometer-scale survey area. We discuss the state-of-the-art of many less mature aspects of SDF below. 2.3.1 SDF and autonomy The software framework that supports the SDF implementation at LBNL is named the Robotic Operating System (ROS) [32]. ROS was designed to facilitate online message passing between sensors, algorithms, and robotic control systems and as a result, ROS- based SDF software is inherently compatible with many robotics control systems including UAVs and ground-based robots. The first fully-integrated instance of SDF-driven autonomy leveraged the PSL algorithm for inputs to onboard real-time autonomous navigation algorithm controlled by the LAMP computer. Fig. 7 shows an few images where a UAV carrying a LAMP payload flying at 13 m above ground level (AGL) is provided a pre-programmed survey pattern (shown in green in Figure 3), which was to take the UAV approximately 6 m from the source at closest approach. However, when the PSL algorithm achieves a preset level of confidence that a source is present (which occurs at approximately 12m horizontal offset), the navigation algorithm enters a ‘stage 1’ locate mode and replaces the pre-programmed way-point with the predicted source position. The top graphic of Fig. 7 shows the PSL map and UAV trajectory at the moment this preset level was exceeded.
